consensus_summary: A disciple is a committed learner and follower of Jesus who abides in his teaching, obeys him, bears fruit, accepts self-denial, and grows into his likeness; mainstream usage generally applies this identity to genuine Christians.
book_summary: A disciple is one who perseveres under the Master until divine teaching is inwardly sealed and produces obedience, having entered the Name, accepted discipleship’s cost, and been formed into the Master’s likeness.
consensus_core_identification: A committed learner-follower of Jesus being formed through obedience into his likeness.
book_core_identification: A persevering, obedient learner under the Master who is inwardly formed into the Master’s likeness.
boundary_disagreement: The book makes continuance, inward inscription of the law, obedient fruit, acceptance of cost, and formation toward perfected likeness defining marks. This potentially excludes merely initial, nominal, or nonpersevering believers whom a broad equation of disciple with any believer might include. It does not replace the follower-learner referent.
material_contradiction: There is no central contradiction. The only material tension concerns whether every believer may be called a disciple immediately or whether the designation properly applies to those who continue and manifest costly obedience and fruit.
rationale: Reduced to their minimum cores, both identify the disciple as a follower under Jesus’ instruction who obeys and becomes like the teacher. The book’s language materially sharpens the boundary by presenting perseverance and resulting inward and outward transformation as constitutive, rather than merely expected features of the general Christian identity. This is a narrowing within the recognized discipleship category, not a new or competing referent.
strongest_objection: The entry may be only a poetic restatement of the consensus rather than a true narrowing: John 8:31, Luke 14, and Luke 6:40 are already standard consensus texts for abiding, costly, transformative discipleship. Moreover, the book’s common-view note still describes discipleship as applying to any believer. The subset judgment therefore depends on reading the entry’s conditions as boundaries rather than ideals.
